readerTitle: Should you take the job? Ask two questions first.
caseNote: 가상 사례 (주택 전기 시공업체의 전기기사, 대형 소매기업 재무팀의 분석가) · 적용 레슨: 커리어 자본 + 자기 인식
insight: 이직 제안은 '연봉 비교'가 아니라 '무엇을 배우게 되는가(커리어 자본)'와 '내가 그 일을 잘해낼 사람인가(자기 인식)'라는 두 질문으로 판단한다.
misconception: 연봉이 높거나 회사가 투자하는 부서라면 좋은 제안이다. 일이 맞을지는 들어가 봐야 안다.

sources.text: Newport, C. (2012). So Good They Can't Ignore You. 'career capital' 개념
PIXO 유닛 PPL-01 개념 레슨 (PPL-01-01 자기 인식, PPL-01-06 커리어 자본)
모든 인물과 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 'career capital' 용어는 Cal Newport(2012)에서 널리 알려졌습니다. 카드 본문에는 저자 이름을 쓰지 않았고, 개념 정의가 PPL-01-06 레슨과 일치하는지 확인하세요.
Maya의 연봉 차이 $10,000, 6인 업체, Dev 사례는 모두 가상입니다. 실제 통계나 연구는 인용하지 않았습니다.
6번 카드의 '많은 이직은 1~2년 안에 되돌릴 수 있다'는 일반적 서술입니다. 업종·국가별로 다를 수 있어 단정적 표현을 피했는지 확인하세요.

cards.title: Should you take the job? Ask two questions first.
body: Maya is the lead electrician at a six-person home-repair firm. A regional contractor has offered her a job as an estimator: $10,000 more a year, regular hours, mostly at a desk.
Her boss says she'll be missed. Her partner says take the money. She has until Friday to decide.

image.label: An electrician at a kitchen table with two offer letters
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 작업복 차림의 여성 전기기사가 부엌 식탁에 앉아 두 장의 제안서를 양손에 들고 고민하는 장면. 식탁 위에 공구 가방과 달력(금요일에 동그라미). 실제 회사 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Where should Maya start?
body: Before comparing benefits and commute times, she wants one question that cuts through the noise. Which one?

options.text: Which job pays more over the next five years?
options.feedback: Pay matters, and it's the easiest number to compare. But it says nothing about what she'd get better at, or whether she'd stay long enough to collect it.

options.text: Which job builds skills that are rare and useful for where I want to go?
options.feedback: This is **career capital**: skills that make you valuable and give you more choices later. It turns a job offer into an investment question.

options.text: Which team seemed nicer in the interview?
options.feedback: People matter a lot. But interviews show everyone at their best, and a friendly team can still teach you very little.

cards.title: What would she be learning?
body: Maya has said for years she wants her own firm someday. Today she's excellent at the wiring, but she rarely prices a job or wins a bid. The owner does that.
As an estimator, she'd read plans, price materials and labor, and see which bids win and why. That is the exact gap between a great electrician and someone who can run a shop.
The extra $10,000 is nice. The **skills** may be worth more.

image.label: Two columns: skills she has vs skills the new role adds
image.brief: 두 칸 비교 인포그래픽. 왼쪽 'Skills she has': 배선, 설치, 고객 응대. 오른쪽 'Skills the role adds': 도면 읽기, 견적 계산, 입찰. 오른쪽 칸에서 화살표가 '내 가게' 아이콘으로 이어짐. 로고 없음.

cards.title: Will she actually like a desk job?
body: The role builds useful skills. But a job she dreads won't last long enough to pay off. How should she check whether it fits her?

options.text: Trust her gut. She'll know after the first week.
options.feedback: Gut feelings carry real information, but in week one everything is new. And by then she has already left her old job.

options.text: Look back at which tasks she's volunteered for and which drained her, and ask a coworker what they've seen.
options.feedback: This is **self-awareness** built on evidence. Past behavior plus an honest outside view beats how a job sounds on paper.

options.text: Ask the hiring manager what the job is really like.
options.feedback: She'll get useful facts, but the manager is selling. They can describe the job, not tell her about herself.

cards.title: The pattern she'd missed.
body: Maya looks back at the past year. She loved the jobs where she worked out a tricky problem with a customer. She dreaded the weeks of repetitive installs.
Estimating is mostly problem-solving: why this house needs a panel upgrade, what the inspector will flag. A coworker adds, "You're the one who always does the quote math in your head."
The desk sounded wrong. The **work itself** fits her.

cards.title: Neither lens decides alone.
body: Career capital can become an excuse to accept poor pay or poor treatment "for the experience." If the money doesn't cover the bills, new skills won't fix that.
Self-awareness has limits too. Past patterns guide you, but people often grow into roles they'd never have picked. Treat both as evidence, not verdicts.
Also ask what a mistake would cost. Many job moves can be undone within a year or two.

cards.title: Now it's a move inside a big company.
body: Dev is a financial analyst at a large retailer. The company's app team asks him to join as a product analyst: same pay, new manager, faster pace.
He loves his current manager. He does his best work in long, quiet stretches. What should he do?

image.label: An analyst between a finance desk and a busy app team
image.brief: 사무실 한 층을 위에서 본 장면. 왼쪽은 조용한 재무팀 책상(스프레드시트 화면), 오른쪽은 화이트보드와 휴대폰 앱 화면 시안이 붙은 북적이는 앱 팀. 가운데 복도에 남성 분석가가 서서 양쪽을 바라봄. 실제 기업 로고 없음.

options.text: Move. The app team is where the company is investing.
options.feedback: Following investment can build career capital, but it skips two questions: which skills this role actually builds, and whether he'll do well there.

options.text: Ask what he'd be able to do in 18 months that he can't now, and how much quiet focus the work allows.
options.feedback: Both lenses at once: **career capital** (which rare skills he gains) and **self-awareness** (how he works best). Now he's comparing jobs, not reputations.

options.text: Stay. A great manager is hard to find.
options.feedback: A great manager is valuable, but staying for one person is fragile. Managers move on too, and he may already have stopped learning.

cards.title: Take the job that makes you more valuable, and that you'll do well in.
body: Concepts used: **career capital** (which rare, useful skills a role builds) and **self-awareness** (evidence about how you work best). Pay, people and pace still matter. These two questions help you weigh them.
**Try it today:** write down three tasks from the past month you did well and enjoyed, and three that drained you. Hold your next offer up against that list.
